how-much-to-charge-for-foundation-repair.text:
← Foundation repair bid calculator

How much to charge for foundation repair

The number a homeowner wants is a price per pier. That number is not a takeoff. An 8-pier brochure house with exterior access is not the same job as a 6-pier interior house with an engineering stamp and four carbon-fiber straps. The pier count is smaller on the interior house. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count access and extra shaft, not just piers

Helical piers screw to a torque number. Hydraulic push piers drive to refusal. Bowed-wall work is carbon-fiber straps or steel I-beams and does not invent a pier count. Waterproofing prices French drain and a sump. A retaining wall prices height and geogrid. Foundation repair prices settlement and a wall that is moving. Quoting all three from a published per-pier number is how the first cramped interior bracket eats the field margin.

A house with fewer piers can cost more

Each interior bracket is typically a crawl or basement setup, a different bracket, and hours that never appear in the pier count. Extra shaft past the footage already in the pier price is billed by the foot. An engineering stamp and a plumbing reroute under the slab are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 6-pier interior helical house at 14 ft with four carbon-fiber straps, an engineering stamp, and a plumbing reroute prices about $14,803 ($2,467 per pier, 50.9 crew-hours). The same shop’s 8-pier exterior helical job at 12 ft prices about $9,489 ($1,186 per pier, 29.9 hours, walk-away $6,832). Matching the brochure job’s per-pier number on the interior house is how that job becomes a loss.

Push piers and straps are not a markup on helical

Push piers drive faster and usually cost less per pier than helical, until the lot has no equipment path. On the sample rates a 10-pier push job at 16 ft with poor lot access prices about $11,856 ($1,186 per pier, 34.1 crew-hours) — more hours than the 8-pier helical brochure job, not because there are more sticks in the ground but because the machine cannot get to them. A bowed-wall-only job of eight carbon-fiber straps with an engineering stamp and no piers prices about $7,186 (27.9 hours). Treating either as a blended “add 20%” is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first stuck drive.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $42/h tech loaded at 34% payroll burden is $56.28. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a structural-engineering specification, a settlement warranty, a soil-performance guarantee, a permit, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Soil, pier depth, bracket type, and whether the wall needs straps are yours to confirm.

Price your foundation

Common questions

How much to charge for foundation repair?

Charge from pier count, installed depth past the footage already in the pier price, interior versus exterior access, engineering stamp, carbon-fiber straps, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 8-pier exterior helical job at 12 ft prices around $9,489 on the sample rates in this calculator — about $1,186 per pier.

Why is a per-pier foundation quote dangerous?

Homeowners count piers. Interior brackets, extra shaft, an engineering stamp, and carbon-fiber straps on a bowed wall do not scale with that count. Matching a cheaper per-pier quote written for an exterior brochure house is how an interior-access job becomes a week-long loss.

Does a house with fewer piers always cost less to repair?

No. On the sample rates a 6-pier interior helical house with 14 ft of depth, an engineering stamp, four carbon-fiber straps, and a plumbing reroute prices around $14,803 ($2,467 per pier), while a longer 8-pier exterior brochure job at 12 ft prices around $9,489 ($1,186 per pier).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not structural-engineering, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a settlement warranty, or an engineering specification — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Common questions

      Why can a competitor advertise a flat “price per pier”?

      Usually because the quote is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: 8 exterior helical piers at 12 feet deep with easy access — the brochure job. It really does price low. What the per-pier number cannot see is interior access, depth past what is included, an engineering stamp, wall straps, and a plumbing reroute. Price your actual foundation beside the quote and the gap becomes a list of line items instead of an argument about who is honest.

      Why does interior access cost more than exterior for the same pier count?

      Because interior brackets mean working inside a finished or semi-finished basement — cramped clearance under joists, protecting floors and walls, and sometimes routing plumbing out of the way before a pier bracket can even go in. Exterior piers are set from open ground with equipment that cannot fit inside a house. Same pier, same depth, very different working conditions.

      Why does depth past 10 feet add cost per pier instead of a flat per-pier rate?

      Because each method’s per-pier price already includes a starting depth — 10 feet for both helical and push piers here — and every foot past that is additional drive time and additional pier segments, billed per foot rather than absorbed into the base price. A 16-foot pier in poor soil is not the same job as a 10-foot pier just because the brochure quoted “$X per pier.”

      Is this the same as basement waterproofing or a concrete slab job?

      No. This prices holding a settled or bowed foundation up and still — piers, extra shaft depth, interior access, engineering, and wall straps. It is distinct from basement waterproofing (a French drain, a sump pit, and a discharge line for water, not structure), new concrete pours, retaining walls (height and geogrid on a wall you are building), and crawl space encapsulation. A bowed wall with no settlement may only need straps or I-beams, priced here with zero piers.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us; your bid is also saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your pier count, wages, or prices.

      What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

      The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — piers, extra depth, access, engineering, and wall straps — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

vs-a-flat-price-per-pier.html.text:
← Foundation Repair Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per pier

Foundation-repair contractors are shopped by a flat price per pier. That rate cannot see the job — interior access, extra shaft depth, an engineering stamp, and carbon-fiber straps do not scale with pier count, and a 6-pier job can take more crew-hours than an 8-pier job of the same method.

What a flat price per pier is

A price per pier is the fastest number to quote over the phone: count the piers, multiply by a rate, read back a total. It is also the unit homeowners already compare between competing bids, and the unit a lot of estimator sheets carry forward from job to job.

The rate behind it was learned from a specific job — a given access, depth, and scope — and then reused for the next pier count that calls in, whether or not that next job shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter pier method and count, average installed depth, depth included in the pier price, interior versus exterior access, poor lot access, an engineering stamp, carbon-fiber straps, steel I-beams, grade beam, slab jacking, and a plumbing reroute, plus your own wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin. It prices piers, extra depth, interior brackets, access, wall straps, and engineering as their own hours and cost lines — for this job, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat per-pier rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for an exterior bracket in open dirt and an interior bracket under a finished floor, even though interior access is its own labor. Prices interior-access hours separately per pier, so an interior job costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for depth past what a published price includes — a 12 ft pier and an 18 ft pier of the same method get the same rate. Prices extra shaft depth past the included footage as its own hours and material, per pier.
Has no line for an engineering stamp or coordinating one, even though an interior or structural job usually needs it. Prices the engineering stamp fee and the hours to coordinate it as their own line.
Has no line for carbon-fiber straps, steel I-beams, a grade beam, slab jacking, or a plumbing reroute at all. Prices each of those as its own hours and material, on top of the pier count.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per pier and the walk-away price alongside the total, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same method, two different jobs

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $42 hourly wage, 34% burden, $420 per pier and bracket, $18 per extra foot of shaft, $95 per interior bracket, $185 per carbon-fiber strap, an $850 engineering fee, a $650 plumbing allowance, $285 travel and equipment, 16% overhead, 28% target margin:

An 8-pier helical job with exterior access, 12 ft average depth, no engineering stamp, and no straps takes 29.9 crew-hours and prices at $9,488.87 for the job — $1,186.11 per pier.

A 6-pier helical job with interior access, 14 ft average depth, an engineering stamp, four carbon-fiber straps, and a plumbing reroute — fewer piers, harder job — takes 50.9 crew-hours, costs $10,657.82 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $14,802.53 — $2,467.09 per pier. Quoting the interior job at the exterior job's learned rate of $1,186.11 per pier gives $7,116.66 for six piers, which is $3,541.17 below the interior job's own break-even cost — before counting the $7,685.87 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 28% target margin. Fewer piers, more crew-hours, and a rate learned on the easier job loses money the moment the crew is under the house.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per pier get a foundation-repair bid wrong?

Because pier count only measures how many piers, not what each one costs to install. An 8-pier job with exterior access, 12 ft average depth, and no engineering takes about 29.9 crew-hours. A 6-pier job with interior brackets, 14 ft average depth, an engineering stamp, and four carbon-fiber straps takes about 50.9 crew-hours -- fewer piers, far more labor, because access, extra depth, engineering, and wall straps do not scale with pier count.

What does a flat per-pier rate usually miss entirely?

Interior access, extra shaft depth past what a published price includes, an engineering stamp, carbon-fiber straps, and a plumbing reroute under the slab. A flat rate has no line for the difference between an exterior bracket in open dirt and an interior bracket under a finished floor, no line for depth beyond the included footage, no line for the stamp and coordination an interior or structural job usually needs, and no line for wall straps or a plumbing reroute at all.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs: an 8-pier exterior job at 12 ft average depth, no interior access, no engineering, takes 29.9 crew-hours and prices at $9,488.87 -- $1,186.11 per pier. A 6-pier interior job at 14 ft average depth, with an engineering stamp, four carbon-fiber straps, and a plumbing reroute, takes 50.9 crew-hours, costs $10,657.82 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $14,802.53 -- $2,467.09 per pier. Quoting the interior job at the exterior job's learned rate of $1,186.11 per pier gives $7,116.66 for six piers, which is $3,541.17 below the interior job's own break-even cost -- before counting the $7,685.87 it falls short of this calculator's price at a 28% target margin.

Is a flat price per pier ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- the same access, a similar average depth, and no engineering stamp or wall straps -- a per-pier number can land close. The risk is quoting an interior job, extra shaft depth, an engineering stamp, or wall straps the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the access, the depth, the stamp, or the straps until the crew is under the house, and by then the per-pier number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supplier's pier, bracket, or strap pricing. It takes pier count, average depth, interior versus exterior access, engineering, carbon-fiber straps, steel I-beams, grade beam, slab jacking, and plumbing reroute, plus your own wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into crew-hours and a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-pier rate skips, not a market survey.

Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and material costs, and against a licensed structural engineer, before relying on it or submitting a bid. This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this foundation-repair job cost, given its piers, depth, and access, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes pier method and count, extra shaft depth past what is included, interior versus exterior access, an engineering stamp, carbon-fiber straps, steel I-beams, a grade beam, slab jacking, a plumbing reroute, plus loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money and a copyable customer-facing bid summary — plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block.
